family_lesson.where_to_look_first: Go to the reproductive center: look for numerous free stamens and one to many mostly free carpels on a superior ovary/receptacle, with floral parts generally not fused into a Rosaceae-style hypanthium.
core_characters: Carpels commonly several to many and free (apocarpous), although family variation exists.
Sepals are free and often petaloid.
Petals may be present, reduced, highly modified, or absent.
Fruit commonly an aggregate of achenes or follicles.
Leaves commonly lack true stipules; most genera have alternate leaves, while Clematis has opposite leaves.
local_variation: Aquilegia canadensis: 5 petaloid sepals + 5 nectar-bearing spurred petals; several follicles at fruit.
Clematis: petals absent; showy structures are petaloid sepals; many free stamens; fruits are aggregates of achenes, commonly with persistent elongated styles.
Clematis drummondii is dioecious in local detailed descriptions: male and female flowers occur on separate plants.

Rosaceae.confusion: Can also have numerous stamens and multiple free carpels.
Rosaceae.tie_breaker: Rosaceae commonly has a conspicuous hypanthium and stipules; Ranunculaceae flowers are typically hypogynous with stamens/carpels inserted directly on the receptacle and usually lack stipules.

Papaveraceae.confusion: Showy flowers with numerous stamens can look superficially similar.
Papaveraceae.tie_breaker: Papaveraceae commonly has 2 early-deciduous sepals, 4 petals, latex, and a syncarpous capsule; Ranunculaceae usually has free carpels or an aggregate fruit.

cards.look_here_first: Turn the nodding flower sideways. Find five long nectar spurs pointing backward from the petals.
confirm: Five petaloid sepals form the outer red showy whorl.
Five petals each narrow into a long basal nectar spur.
Numerous free stamens surround several free pistils.
Fruit is a cluster of several follicles rather than an achene head.
Leaves are divided into rounded, lobed leaflets; Central Texas plants occupy limestone canyon/ledge habitats.
cards.family_teaching_value: Shows the 'petals present and highly modified' side of Ranunculaceae, balancing petal-less Clematis.

cards.common_name: old man's beard / Texas virgin's bower
cards.look_here_first: First decide whether you are looking at a flower or a fruiting head. Flowers have four cream/white petaloid sepals; female plants later produce enormous silky plumose achene masses.
confirm: Perennial climbing vine using petioles/petiolules to twine around supports.
Flowers lack petals; the showy structures are 4 free petaloid sepals.
Local detailed descriptions treat the species as dioecious: staminate flowers have many free stamens; pistillate flowers have many free pistils.
Each achene retains an elongated feathery/plumose style, producing the characteristic old-man's-beard infructescence.
confusions: other native Clematis when not flowering
cards.tie_breaker: Against introduced C. terniflora, combine the divided/lobed foliage, dioecious 4-sepal flowers and exceptionally long silky plumose fruiting heads rather than relying on white flower color.

cards.look_here_first: Look at the thick sepals in side view: four leathery scarlet/rose sepals form a nodding urn and flare/recurve sharply at their tips.
confirm: Woody-based perennial climber with opposite pinnately compound leaves.
Terminal leaflet or leaflet axis can function as a tendril.
Petals absent; four thick petaloid sepals form the conspicuous urn-shaped flower.
Sepal margins are not broadly expanded and crispate as in the typical Pitcher's-leatherflower look; tips are sharply recurved.
Fruit is an aggregate of achenes with persistent style/beak structures.
cards.tie_breaker: C. texensis has thick true scarlet/rose urn-shaped sepals with strongly recurved tips; C. pitcheri is usually purple and its distal sepal margins are more expanded/crispate or recurved.

comparison_module.title: Clematis in Central Texas — structure before color
sequence: Open flower or nodding leathery urn?
Open cream/white 4-sepal flower + dioecious + huge plumose fruit masses → C. drummondii.
Nodding thick leatherflower → compare C. texensis vs C. pitcheri by sepal shape/margin/tip, not just color.
Masses of small open white flowers + introduced status → consider C. terniflora.
taxonomy_guardrails: Do not use old broad C. reticulata records as current Central Texas evidence without re-identification.
C. terniflora is introduced in Texas and remains an encounter-value comparison, not a native-family anchor.
